subject: Medical Terminology
title: Lecture 14 and 15 - Blood and Lymphatic System

A.q: What are the liquid and cellular parts of blood?
options: Serum; red cells, white cells, platelets
Plasma; red cells, white cells, platelets
A.explain: Blood is liquid plasma plus formed elements: erythrocytes (red cells), leukocytes (white cells), and thrombocytes (platelets). Serum is plasma after clotting, lymph is lymphatic fluid, and lymphocytes and monocytes are only two white-cell types.

A.q: Which duties belong to the lymphatic system, not blood?
options: Filtering particles, immunity, fluid balance, fat absorption
Delivering oxygen and hormones, removing metabolic wastes
Driving the flow, working valves, perfusing the heart
Making blood cells, storing calcium, anchoring muscles
A.explain: The lymphatic system filters foreign particles, sustains immune responses, balances tissue fluid, and absorbs dietary fats. Delivery and waste removal are blood duties, pumping is the heart, and making cells and storing calcium is bone.

A.q: How do plasma and serum differ?
options: Serum keeps clotting factors; plasma remains after clotting
Both lack clotting factors; differ in red cells
Both hold clotting factors; differ in proteins
Plasma keeps clotting factors; serum remains after clotting
A.explain: Plasma still holds fibrinogen and the other clotting factors; serum is the fluid left after blood clots. They do not differ by red cells or other proteins.

A.q: What kind of substance is hemoglobin, the pigment in red cells?
options: Respiratory pigment: protein with calcium compound
Storage pigment: protein with iron-protein compound
Respiratory pigment: protein with iron compound
Visual pigment: protein with retinal compound
A.explain: Hemoglobin is a respiratory pigment made of a protein (globin) bound to an iron compound (heme). Storage iron is ferritin and the visual pigment is rhodopsin.

A.q: How do granulocytes and agranulocytes differ?
options: Granulocytes: lobed nuclei, granules; agranulocytes: one nucleus, none
Granulocytes: one nucleus, no granules; agranulocytes: lobed, granules
Granulocytes: in marrow; agranulocytes: in intestinal lining
Granulocytes: make antibodies; agranulocytes: phagocytose germs
A.explain: Granulocytes have lobed nuclei and visible granules; agranulocytes have a single nucleus and no granules. Location and antibody production do not separate them.

A.q: A granulocyte that fights infection by phagocytosis and is the most common white cell is which type?
A.explain: The neutrophil is the granulocyte whose cytoplasmic granules take a neutral stain and that clears infection by phagocytosis, with a lifespan of up to about 24 hours. The eosinophil stains orange to rosy. The basophil stains dark blue. The monocyte also phagocytoses for about a day but is an agranulocyte with no granules.

A.q: Which white cell stains dark blue, takes part in immune surveillance, and releases anticoagulants to inflamed tissue?
A.explain: The basophil is the short-lived granulocyte, usually under two days, that stains dark blue, contributes to immune surveillance, and brings anticoagulant substances to inflamed tissues. The neutrophil stains neutral. The eosinophil stains orange to rosy. The lymphocyte is an agranulocyte active in adaptive immunity.

A.q: Which white cell stains bright yellow-red to orange and increases during parasitic infection and allergic reactions?
A.explain: The eosinophil is the granulocyte that stains bright yellow-red, orange, or rosy and whose count rises during parasitic infections and allergic reactions, with a lifespan of about two to five days. The basophil stains dark blue. The neutrophil stains neutral. The monocyte is a non-granular phagocyte.

A.q: What do the parts of polymorphonuclear (granulocytes) mean?
options: One, form, center: single round nucleus
A.explain: Poly means many, morpho form, and nucleus kernel, so polymorphonuclear describes the many-lobed nucleus of granulocytes.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte matures under thymic influence and attacks foreign cells, cancer cells, and virus-infected cells?
A.explain: The T-cell matures under thymic influence and attacks foreign cells, cancer cells, and virus-infected cells. The B-cell makes antibodies, the NK-cell kills through cytotoxic substances, and the monocyte is a phagocyte, not a lymphocyte.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte arises in the bone marrow?
A.explain: The B-cell arises in the bone marrow and makes antibodies against antigens. The T-cell matures under thymic influence, the NK-cell kills through cytotoxic substances, and the monocyte is a phagocyte, not a lymphocyte.

A.q: Which type of lymphocyte destroys tumor or infected cells through cytotoxic substances?
A.explain: The NK-cell, or natural killer cell, carries cytotoxic substances that kill tumor or infected cells. The T-cell attacks cells after maturing in the thymus, the B-cell makes antibodies, and the monocyte is a phagocyte, not a lymphocyte.

A.q: What is immunity, as a physiological mechanism?
options: Pumping blood out to tissues and back again
Recognizing and removing foreign material harmlessly
Filtering old red cells and storing their iron
Absorbing dietary fats into the circulating bloodstream
A.explain: Immunity is the ability to recognize foreign materials and neutralize or remove them without harming the body. Pumping is the heart, filtering red cells is the spleen, and fat absorption is the lacteals.

A.q: Which defines antigen and antibody correctly?
options: Antigen: Y-shaped protein; antibody: the invading substance
Both: foreign substances entering from outside the body
Antigen: provokes antibodies; antibody: Y-shaped neutralizing protein
Antigen: B-cell made protein; antibody: NK-cell cytotoxic substance
A.explain: An antigen is any substance that provokes antibody formation; an antibody is the Y-shaped protein that inactivates it. Antibodies are made by B cells, and cytotoxic substances belong to NK cells.

A.q: How do active and passive immunity differ?
options: Active: long-lasting, self-made; passive: short, received
Active: short, received; passive: long-lasting, self-made
Active: long-lasting, received; passive: short, self-made
A.explain: Active immunity is long-lasting and made by the body itself; passive immunity is short-lasting and received from outside, as maternal antibodies are.

A.q: How do natural and artificial active immunity differ?
A.explain: Natural active immunity follows an infection; artificial active immunity follows a vaccine. Serum and breast milk give passive immunity.

A.q: How do natural and artificial passive immunity differ?
options: Natural: after vaccine; artificial: after infection recovery
Natural: placenta, breast milk; artificial: injected serum
Natural: built by host; artificial: built after vaccine
Both: long-lasting, from the host memory cells
A.explain: Natural passive immunity passes through the placenta and breast milk; artificial passive immunity is injected serum. Both are short-lived and not built by the host.

A.q: In the term hemochromatosis, the element chrom refers to what?
A.explain: The term splits into hem/o meaning blood, chrom meaning color, and the suffix -osis meaning a condition, so chrom contributes the sense of color, as in the pigment or iron-color deposits of hemochromatosis. Blood is carried by the hem element of the same word. Clot and spleen belong to thromb/o and splen/o, which do not appear here.

A.q: In the term thrombophlebitis, the element thrombo refers to what?
A.explain: The term joins thrombo meaning clot, phleb meaning vein, and the suffix -itis meaning inflammation, so thrombo contributes the sense of clot. Vein is the phleb element of the same word. Color and blood belong to chrom/o and hem/o, neither of which is present.

A.q: In the term lymphoduct, the element lympho refers to what?
A.explain: Lympho is the combining form for the clear fluid lymph, so in lymphoduct it names that fluid and the term means a duct carrying lymph. Thymus, spleen, and color are the senses of thym/o, splen/o, and chrom/o.

A.q: What does the term hematocytopenia mean?
A.explain: Hematocytopenia is built from Hemat/o (blood), cyt/o (cell), and -penia (deficiency), so it denotes a deficiency of blood cells. An excess would use -osis or -cytosis, a platelet deficiency is thrombocytopenia, and clotting-factor excess is not the sense of this term.

A.q: What does the term splenomegaly mean?
A.explain: Splenomegaly is built from Splen/o (spleen) and -megaly (enlargement), so it denotes an enlarged spleen. Inflammation would use -itis, removal would use -ectomy, and pain would use -dynia.

A.q: What does the term thrombophlebitis mean?
options: Inflammation of an artery caused by a clot
Inflammation of a vein caused by a clot
Hardening of a vein caused by a clot
Surgical removal of a clot from a vein
A.explain: Thrombophlebitis is built from Thromb/o (clot), phleb (vein), and -itis (inflammation), so it denotes inflammation of a vein caused by a clot. The other options keep part of the term but change another word part, so they do not match.

A.q: What does the term thymocyte mean?
options: A cell of the bone marrow
A cell of the lymph node
A.explain: Thymocyte is built from Thym/o (thymus) and -cyte (cell), so it denotes a cell of the thymus. Spleen cells would use Splen/o, bone marrow cells would use Myel/o, and lymph node cells would use Lymph/o.

A.q: What does the term athymism mean?
A.explain: Athymism is built from the prefix a- (without), Thym/o (thymus), and -ism (condition), so it denotes the absence of the thymus. Enlargement would use -megaly, inflammation would use -itis, and surgical removal would use -ectomy.

A.q: What does the term immunopharmacology mean?
options: Study of drugs acting on immunity
Study of immune cells in blood
Study of immune response to infection
Treatment of immune disorders without drugs
A.explain: Immunopharmacology is immun/o + pharmac/o (drug) + -logy: the study of drugs that act on the immune system.

A.q: What does the term hemochromatosis mean?
options: A condition of excess blood cells
A condition of excessive iron deposits
A condition of deficient blood clotting
A condition of excess clots in the veins
A.explain: Hemochromatosis is built from Hem/o (blood), chromat/o (color), and -osis (condition), so it denotes a condition involving excessive iron deposits and the resulting skin color changes. Excess blood cells would use -cytosis, deficient clotting would use a different suffix, and excess clots in veins is thrombophlebitis.

A.q: Which structure is the lymphoid organ that produces T-lymphocytes to fight off foreign organisms?
A.explain: The thymus produces T-lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms. The spleen filters old blood cells, the tonsils trap pathogens from food and air, and the appendix helps house good bacteria.

A.q: Which structure filters and removes old and damaged blood cells and fights infection and disease?
A.explain: The spleen filters and removes old and damaged blood cells and fights infection and disease. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the bone marrow produces blood cells, and the Peyer's patches monitor and destroy bacteria in the small intestine.

A.q: Which structures trap pathogens from food and air as a first defense?
options: The Peyer's patches and lymph nodes
A.explain: The tonsils and adenoid trap pathogens from food and air, the first line of defense. The thymus makes T cells, the spleen filters blood, the marrow forms cells, and Peyer's patches guard the intestine.

A.q: Which structure produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets?
A.explain: The bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters old blood cells, and the tonsils trap pathogens.

A.q: Which structures are found in the lining of the small intestine and monitor and destroy bacteria?
A.explain: The Peyer's patches are found in the lining of the small intestine and monitor and destroy bacteria. The tonsils and adenoids trap pathogens from food and air, and the appendix plays a role in housing good bacteria.

A.q: Which structure plays a role in housing good bacteria?
A.explain: The appendix plays a role in housing good bacteria. The thymus produces T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters old blood cells, and the tonsils trap pathogens from food and air.

A.q: Which fluid is the colorless, watery liquid collected from the body tissues and moved back into the bloodstream?
A.explain: Lymph is the colorless, watery fluid collected from the body tissues and moved back into the circulatory system by the lymphatic network. Plasma and serum are blood fractions, and interstitial fluid is the tissue fluid before it enters the lymphatic capillaries.

A.q: How are interstitial fluid and lymph related?
options: Lymph is that fluid in blood capillaries
Lymph is that fluid in lymphatic capillaries
Lymph is that fluid leaving nodes for veins
Lymph is a separate fluid made in nodes
A.explain: Interstitial fluid lies between tissue cells; once it enters lymphatic capillaries it is called lymph.

A.q: What do the valves in lymphatic vessels do?
options: Stop lymph flowing back to tissues
Keep lymph out of the blood
A.explain: Lymphatic valves stop lymph from flowing backward. They do not pump, allow two-way flow, or keep lymph from the blood.

A.q: How does lymph flow through a lymph node?
options: In by efferent, out by afferent
In by afferent, out by efferent
In and out by afferent only
In by one duct, out by another
A.explain: Lymph enters a node through afferent vessels and leaves through efferent vessels. The ducts drain lymph into veins, not through a node.

A.q: What path returns lymph to the bloodstream?
options: Lymph capillaries, nodes, ducts, then veins
Lymph nodes, capillaries, ducts, then veins
Lymph capillaries, nodes, then right atrium
Lymph capillaries, nodes, then portal vein
A.explain: Lymph enters lymphatic capillaries, passes through lymph nodes, and returns to the veins through the lymphatic ducts.

A.q: Match each type of blood cell to the feature that defines it.
A.explain: Erythrocytes carry oxygen and carbon dioxide on hemoglobin. Neutrophils have neutral granules and phagocytose; basophils have dark blue granules and release anticoagulants; eosinophils have orange-rosy granules and rise in parasitic and allergic states. Monocytes are phagocytic agranulocytes; thrombocytes are megakaryocyte fragments for clotting.

A.q: Match each type of lymphocyte to the feature that defines it.
A.explain: T cells mature under the thymus and attack foreign, cancerous, and virus-infected cells. B cells arise in marrow and make antibodies. NK cells are natural killers carrying cytotoxic substances.

A.q: Match each lymphatic organ to the role it performs.
A.explain: The thymus generates T cells, the spleen removes aged blood cells and fights infection, the tonsils and adenoids trap pathogens from food and air, bone marrow forms all blood cells, Peyer's patches guard the small intestine, and the appendix houses good bacteria.

A.q: Match each combining form to the structure or idea it denotes.
A.explain: Chrom/o and Chromat/o both mean color, as in hemochromatosis, Hem/o and Hemat/o both mean blood, as in hematocytopenia, Splen/o means spleen, as in splenomegaly, Thromb/o means clot, as in thrombophlebitis, Immun/o means safe, as in immunopharmacology, and Lymph/o means the clear fluid lymph, as in lymphoduct. The remaining form of this group, Thym/o with Thym/i, means thymus, as in thymocyte and athymism.

A.q: Match each term to its meaning.
A.explain: Hematocytopenia is a blood-cell deficiency, splenomegaly an enlarged spleen, thrombophlebitis vein inflammation with a clot, a thymocyte a thymus cell, and athymism absence of the thymus.

A.q: Match each blood cell to its lifespan.
A.explain: The erythrocyte lives about 110 to 120 days. The neutrophil and the monocyte both live up to about 24 hours, so they share one answer. The basophil usually lives under 2 days, and the eosinophil about 2 to 5 days. The thrombocyte lives about 7 to 10 days. The T cell lives about 30 to 160 days, the B cell about 5 to 6 weeks, and the NK cell up to about 2 weeks.

A.q: Match each immunity route to how long it lasts.
A.explain: Natural active and artificial active immunity are long-lasting, because the host makes its own antibodies. Natural passive and artificial passive immunity are short-lasting, because the antibodies come from another source.

A.q: What do the lymph nodes do?
options: Filter microorganisms and particles from lymph
Collect interstitial fluid to form new lymph
Drain the right head and chest into blood
Stop lymph flowing backward in the vessels
A.explain: Lymph nodes filter microorganisms and foreign particles from lymph. Capillaries collect fluid, the right lymphatic duct drains the right head and chest, and valves stop backflow.

A.q: What do lymphatic capillaries do?
options: Filter the particles inside lymph nodes
Collect interstitial fluid for return to blood
Drain the left upper body into subclavian
Return lymph straight into the right atrium
A.explain: Lymphatic capillaries collect interstitial fluid and begin its return to the blood. Nodes filter, and the thoracic duct drains the left upper body.

A.q: Which areas does the thoracic duct drain into the blood?
options: Lower body and left upper body
Lower body only, into right atrium
Left arm only, into lymph nodes
A.explain: The thoracic duct drains lymph from the lower body and left upper body into the blood. The right lymphatic duct drains the right head, neck, and chest.

A.q: Which areas does the right lymphatic duct drain into the blood?
options: Lower body and left upper body
Right side of head and chest
Right arm only, into the nodes
Both legs, into the right atrium
A.explain: The right lymphatic duct drains the right side of the head and chest into the blood. The thoracic duct drains the lower body and left upper body.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes the role of the thymus in the lymphatic system?
options: It produces B-lymphocytes that manufacture antibodies.
It produces T-lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms.
It produces red blood cells that carry oxygen.
It produces platelets that are essential for clotting.
A.explain: The thymus produces T-lymphocytes that fight off foreign organisms. B-lymphocytes, red cells, and platelets come from the bone marrow.

A.q: What does the bone marrow produce?
A.explain: Bone marrow forms red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

A.q: Where do Peyer's patches monitor and destroy bacteria?
A.explain: Peyer's patches monitor and destroy bacteria in the lining of the small intestine.

A.q: What does the appendix house?
A.explain: The appendix houses good bacteria that support the gut.

A.q: A formed element that contains hemoglobin and carries oxygen and carbon dioxide is which type?
A.explain: This is the erythrocyte, the red cell that contains hemoglobin and carries the respiratory gases. The leukocyte, thrombocyte, and lymphocyte do other work.

A.q: Which is the correct spelling of the most common white cell, a phagocyte?
A.explain: Neutrophil is the most common white cell and fights infection by phagocytosis. The others are misspellings.

A.q: This white cell increases during parasitic infection and allergic reactions. Which is the correct spelling of this cell?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Eosinophil. Eosinophill, Eosinofil, and Eosinaphil are misspellings.

A.q: Which is the correct spelling of the white cell that brings anticoagulants to inflamed tissue?
A.explain: Basophil takes part in immune surveillance and brings anticoagulants to inflamed tissue. The others are misspellings.

A.q: Which single-nucleus, non-granular white cell gives rise to three lineages?
A.explain: The lymphocyte has one large nucleus, no granules, and three lineages (T, B, NK). The monocyte is also agranular but has no lineages; neutrophils and basophils are granulocytes.

A.q: The largest white cell, with no granules, that destroys germs by phagocytosis, is which type?
A.explain: This is the monocyte. The lymphocyte gives rise to lineages, and the neutrophil and eosinophil carry granules.

A.q: A cell fragment shed by the megakaryocyte that is essential for coagulation is which type?
A.explain: This is the thrombocyte, or platelet. The erythrocyte, leukocyte, and monocyte are whole cells with other jobs.

A.q: Which reading of the parts neutr and phil in neutrophil is correct?
options: A color sense, and a clot
A.explain: Neutr means neither, and phil means attraction for, because the granules take neither an acid nor a basic stain.

A.q: Which three lineages arise from the lymphocyte?
A.explain: The lymphocyte gives rise to the T-cell, the B-cell, and the NK-cell. The other sets mix granulocytes, red cells, and platelets.

A.q: Which nucleus pattern belongs to the lymphocyte?
options: Several nuclear lobes and protein granules
No nucleus, as a cell fragment
One large nucleus and no granules
A pigment mass and no nucleus
A.explain: The lymphocyte has one large nucleus and no granules. Lobed nuclei with granules fit the granulocytes, and the platelet and red cell have no nucleus.

A.q: Which germs does the monocyte destroy by phagocytosis?
options: Bacteria only, not viruses or fungi
Viruses only, not bacteria or fungi
A.explain: The monocyte destroys viruses, bacteria, fungi, and protozoa. Each other option names only part of that list.

A.q: Match each white cell to its class.
A.explain: The neutrophil, eosinophil, and basophil carry granules, so they are granulocytes. The lymphocyte and monocyte lack granules, so they are agranulocytes.

A.q: Match each white cell to how its granules stain.
A.explain: Neutrophil granules stain neutral, eosinophil granules bright yellow-red to orange, and basophil granules dark blue to blue-black. The lymphocyte and monocyte have no granules.

A.q: Where does the T-cell mature?
A.explain: The T-cell matures in the thymus, under thymic influence. The B-cell arises in the bone marrow; the spleen and lymph nodes filter but are not where T-cells mature.

A.q: Where does the B-cell arise?
A.explain: The B-cell arises in the bone marrow. The T-cell matures in the thymus, and the spleen and lymph nodes are filtering organs.

A.q: Which payload does the NK-cell carry?
A.explain: The NK-cell carries cytotoxic substances. Antibodies come from B-cells, neutral granules from neutrophils, and anticoagulants from basophils.

A.q: This lymphoid organ produces the lymphocytes that attack foreign organisms. Which is the correct spelling of this organ?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Thymus. Thymous, Thimys, and Thymuss are misspellings.

A.q: Which spells the organ that filters old blood cells and fights infection?
A.explain: The spleen filters out old and damaged blood cells and fights infection. The others are misspellings.

A.q: Which spells the structure that pairs with the tonsils to trap pathogens?
A.explain: The adenoid pairs with the tonsils to trap pathogens from food and air. The others are misspellings.

A.q: Which spells the soft tissue inside bones where blood cells form?
A.explain: Bone marrow fills bone cavities and forms blood cells. The others are misspellings.

A.q: Which spells the small-intestine structures that monitor bacteria?
A.explain: Peyer's patches lie in the small-intestine lining and monitor bacteria. The others are misspellings.

A.q: This structure helps house beneficial bacteria. Which is the correct spelling of this structure?
A.explain: The correct spelling is Appendix. Apendix, Appendex, and Appendixs are misspellings.

A.q: Which parent of platelets resides in the bone marrow?
A.explain: The megakaryocyte resides in the bone marrow and sheds platelets. Lymphoblasts, monoblasts, and erythroblasts give rise to other cells.

A.q: Which real term uses Chrom/o?
A.explain: The real term is Hemochromatosis. Hematocytopenia uses hemat/o and cyt/o, not chrom/o. Chromocytopenia and Chromatophlebitis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Hem/o?
A.explain: The real term is Hematocytopenia. Hemoductosis, Hematosplenitis, and Hemothymism are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Splen/o?
A.explain: The real term is Splenomegaly. Splenoductosis, Splenothymism, and Splenochromatosis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Thromb/o?
A.explain: The real term is Thrombophlebitis. Thrombochromia, Thrombosplenism, and Thromboductosis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Immun/o?
A.explain: The real term is Immunopharmacology. Immunochromatosis, Immunoductosis, and Immunosplenism are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses Lymph/o?
A.explain: The real term is Lymphoduct. Lymphochromia, Lymphothymism, and Lymphosplenosis are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which real term uses the prefix for absence with Thym/o?
A.explain: The real term is Athymism. Athymocytosis, Athymoduct, and Athymochromia are made-up look-alikes, not real terms.

A.q: Which formed element is named for its role in clotting?
A.explain: The thrombocyte shares the clot sense of thromb/o. The erythrocyte, lymphocyte, and monocyte use other forms.

A.q: Match each immunity route to the event that produces it.

rightItems.text: Transfer by placenta and breast milk

A.explain: Natural active immunity follows recovery after an infection, and artificial active immunity follows a vaccine. Natural passive immunity comes by placenta and breast milk, and artificial passive immunity by injected antibody-containing serum.

A.q: Which set of findings belongs to hemochromatosis?
options: Iron deposits, yellow skin, and spleen enlargement
Excess red cells, bronze skin, and vein clots
Fat deposits, bronze skin, and liver cirrhosis
Iron deposits, bronze skin, and liver cirrhosis
A.explain: Hemochromatosis deposits excess iron in the tissues, giving bronze skin pigmentation and cirrhosis of the liver. Each other set swaps in one wrong finding.

A.q: What does RBC stand for?
A.explain: RBC stands for red blood cell. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: What does WBC stand for?
A.explain: WBC stands for white blood cell. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: What does NK stand for?
A.explain: NK stands for natural killer. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: What does SCT stand for?
A.explain: SCT stands for specialized connective tissue. Each wrong option shares the letters but is not the expansion.

A.q: Which two classes divide the white blood cells?
A.explain: White blood cells divide into granulocytes and agranulocytes. Erythrocytes and thrombocytes are not white cells, and B-cells, T-cells, monocytes, and lymphocytes all belong to the agranulocytes.

A.q: Which lifespan belongs to the red blood cell?
A.explain: The red blood cell lives about 110 to 120 days. About 60 to 80 days and about 70 to 90 days fall short of it, and about 2 to 5 days fits the eosinophil.

A.q: Which other name belongs to the red blood cell?
A.explain: The red blood cell is also called the erythrocyte. Leukocyte, thrombocyte, and lymphocyte name other cells.

A.q: Which other name belongs to the white blood cell?
A.explain: The white blood cell is also called the leukocyte. Erythrocyte, thrombocyte, and megakaryocyte name other elements.

A.q: Match each fluid to its description.
A.explain: Plasma is the yellowish blood fraction with clotting factors; serum is what remains after clotting; interstitial fluid bathes cells outside vessels; lymph is the colorless liquid inside lymphatic vessels.

A.q: Which loads does plasma carry besides clotting factors?
options: Lymph, bile, and suspended blood cells
Water and cells, but no proteins
A.explain: Plasma carries water, proteins, and suspended cells. Lymph and bile are not plasma loads, and plasma carries both water and proteins.

A.q: This term names an inherited disorder seen in blood and lymph work-ups.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?
Which tissue changes belong to Hemochromatosis?
options: Bronze skin pigmentation and liver cirrhosis
Bronze skin pigmentation and spleen fibrosis
Yellow skin pigmentation and liver cirrhosis
Pale skin pigmentation and marrow failure
Hem/o, chrom, and a condition ending
Hem/o, chrom, and an inflammation ending
Hemat/o, chrom, and a condition ending
Hem/o, chromat/o, and a tumor ending

A.explain: This term is hemochromatosis. Hemochromotosis, Hemachromatosis, and Hemochromatasis miss the spelling. Iron overload deposits produce bronze skin pigmentation and can cirrhose the liver. Vein redness and clot after catheter injury fits thrombophlebitis, enlargement of the spleen after congestion is splenomegaly, and absence of the thymus from early life is athymism. The elements are hem/o, chrom, and a condition ending. An inflammation ending would make it an inflammation, hemat/o is not the blood form used in this term, and a tumor ending would name a growth.

A.q: This term appears when blood test results are reported.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: Hemat/o, cyt/o, and a deficiency ending
Hemat/o, cyt/o, and an excess ending
Hem/o, cyt/o, and a deficiency ending
Hemat/o, cyst/o, and a deficiency ending

A.explain: This term is hematocytopenia. Hematocytopenya, Hemotocytopenia, and Hematocitopenia miss the spelling. It means a deficiency of blood cells. An excess of blood cells reverses the ending. A deficiency of platelets only would use thromb/o. An excess of clotting factors is not this term. The elements are hemat/o, cyt/o, and a deficiency ending. An excess ending reverses the meaning, hem/o is not the blood form used in this term, and cyst/o means bladder or sac, not cell.

A.q: This term is used when an abdominal organ is examined.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: Splen/o, megal/o, and a condition ending

A.explain: This term is splenomegaly. Splenomegally, Spleenomegaly, and Splenomegaaly miss the spelling. It means enlargement of the spleen. Inflammation of the spleen, removal of the spleen, and absence of the spleen use other endings. The elements are splen/o and an enlargement ending. An inflammation ending or a removal ending names a different change, and splen/o with megal/o and a condition ending is a wrong split.

A.q: This term names a problem found in a limb after a long period of immobility.

steps.prompt: Which is the correct spelling of this term?

options: Inflammation of a vein associated with a clot
Inflammation of an artery associated with a clot
Inflammation of the spleen associated with a clot
Enlargement of a vein associated with a clot
Thromb/o, phleb, and an inflammation ending
Thromb/o, phleb, and an enlargement ending
Thromb/o, arteri, and an inflammation ending
Thrombocyt/o, phleb, and an inflammation ending

A.explain: This term is thrombophlebitis. Thromboflebitis, Thrombophlebittis, and Thrombophlebitus miss the spelling. It means inflammation of a vein associated with a clot, including clot and redness after vein trauma. Inflammation of an artery associated with a clot would use arteri/o. Inflammation of the spleen associated with a clot would use splen/o. Enlargement of a vein associated with a clot uses an enlargement ending, not -itis.
